titulo: Scenario 2 — Code Generation with Claude Code

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: FinStack, a team of 30 .NET developers, has adopted Claude Code to generate, refactor, and test code in a microservices monorepo. The Claude Code configuration (CLAUDE.md, rules, skills, hooks, settings) is shared through git.

The tech lead wrote the team's conventions (naming, layering pattern, use of Result<T> instead of exceptions) in his own ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. In his Claude Code everything comes out right, but the other developers get code that doesn't follow the standard. What is the fix?
opcoes: Ask each developer to copy the content into their own ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md.
Move the conventions to the project CLAUDE.md (./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md), versioned in the repository.
Put the conventions in the CLAUDE.local.md at the repository root.
Create a /conventions skill that developers must invoke at the start of each session.
questoes.explicacao: Hierarchy: user level (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md) is personal; project level (./CLAUDE.md) belongs to the team and is versioned; CLAUDE.local.md is personal and gitignored.
feedbacks: It works at first, but it creates divergent, unversioned copies; any change has to be replicated by hand on 30 machines.
Correct. ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md is personal and applies only on his machine. Team conventions go in the project CLAUDE.md, shared through git.
CLAUDE.local.md is personal and stays out of git (gitignored); the other developers would still be without the rules.
It depends on each developer remembering to invoke it; a convention that should always apply belongs in the project CLAUDE.md, which is loaded automatically.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: FinStack, a team of 30 .NET developers, has adopted Claude Code to generate, refactor, and test code in a microservices monorepo. The Claude Code configuration (CLAUDE.md, rules, skills, hooks, settings) is shared through git.

Two requests reached the person responsible for the configuration: (1) a developer wants Claude Code to use the URL of her personal sandbox in integration tests, without affecting anyone else; (2) part of the team uses another agent that reads AGENTS.md, and the general rules are already in that file. Which TWO actions fulfill the requests? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: Put the sandbox URL in her CLAUDE.local.md, which is personal and doesn't go to git.
Put the sandbox URL in the project CLAUDE.md, in an "Ana's configuration" section.
Copy all the content of AGENTS.md into CLAUDE.md, so Claude Code doesn't depend on the other file.
In the project CLAUDE.md, import the rules with @AGENTS.md, keeping a single source.
Delete CLAUDE.md, since Claude Code reads AGENTS.md and there's no point in keeping both.
questoes.explicacao: CLAUDE.local.md is the project's personal, gitignored layer. AGENTS.md can be imported into CLAUDE.md with @AGENTS.md, keeping a single source.
feedbacks: Correct. A personal project preference goes in CLAUDE.local.md (gitignored).
It mixes personal configuration with team rules and affects every developer (and leaks into the repository).
Duplication that diverges over time; the @import solves this with a single source of truth.
Correct. The @import avoids duplication: both agents read the same rules. With both present, Claude Code uses CLAUDE.md, which pulls in AGENTS.md.
It loses Claude Code's own layer and doesn't address request 1; the recommended pattern is CLAUDE.md importing AGENTS.md.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: FinStack, a team of 30 .NET developers, has adopted Claude Code to generate, refactor, and test code in a microservices monorepo. The Claude Code configuration (CLAUDE.md, rules, skills, hooks, settings) is shared through git.

The test projects are scattered: services/*/tests/, libs/*/Tests/, and a few new tests/ directories appear every month. The team wants Claude Code to follow the testing conventions (xUnit, AAA pattern, Method_Scenario_Result names) only when it is working on tests. What is the BEST approach?
opcoes: Create a CLAUDE.md inside each test directory with the same conventions, since a subdirectory CLAUDE.md loads on demand when those files are read.
Put the testing conventions in the root CLAUDE.md.
Create a /tests skill that developers invoke when they are going to write tests.
Create .claude/rules/tests.md with paths: containing globs of the test files.
questoes.explicacao: Path-scoped rules (.claude/rules/ with a paths: glob) load only when matching files are touched, and they cover future directories.
feedbacks: Duplication that diverges over time and doesn't automatically cover new directories.
It works, but it loads the testing rules in every session, even when nobody is touching tests, wasting context for nothing.
It depends on remembering to invoke it; a rule that is conditional on files is exactly the use case for rules with paths:.
Correct. A convention that spans directories goes in a file in .claude/rules/ with paths:. It covers future directories without duplicating anything.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: FinStack, a team of 30 .NET developers, has adopted Claude Code to generate, refactor, and test code in a microservices monorepo. The Claude Code configuration (CLAUDE.md, rules, skills, hooks, settings) is shared through git.

A developer is going to migrate serialization from Newtonsoft.Json to System.Text.Json across 60 files in 8 services, with custom converters and some known behavioral incompatibilities. How should the developer carry out the work in Claude Code?
opcoes: Start in plan mode and approve the proposed approach before any edits.
Request the migration directly with acceptEdits mode on, so they don't have to approve 60 edits one by one, and review the full diff at the end.
Use bypassPermissions so the task runs uninterrupted until the end.
Go file by file with direct execution, one session per file.
questoes.explicacao: Plan mode for multi-file changes, architectural decisions, multiple valid approaches, and large scope. Direct execution for a targeted, clear fix.
feedbacks: Correct. A multi-file change with decisions about the approach and behavioral risk: the typical case for plan mode, which explores and asks for approval before editing.
It skips the design step in a migration with multiple valid approaches; the volume of automatic edits without an approved plan increases the risk.
bypassPermissions is not routine for a long, uncontained task, and it doesn't address the lack of planning.
It loses the big picture (shared converters, migration order) and multiplies inconsistent decisions across files.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: FinStack, a team of 30 .NET developers, has adopted Claude Code to generate, refactor, and test code in a microservices monorepo. The Claude Code configuration (CLAUDE.md, rules, skills, hooks, settings) is shared through git.

There are several items in the sprint's task queue. Which TWO should start in plan mode instead of direct execution? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: Fix a NullReferenceException whose stack trace points to the exact line in PaymentService.cs.
Add service-to-service authentication, where the team has not yet decided between mTLS and internal JWT tokens.
Change the value of the MaxRetries constant from 3 to 5.
Add a log line at the start of a handler's Handle method.
Reorganize the boundaries between the Billing and Invoicing modules, moving classes between projects.
questoes.explicacao: Plan mode: multi-file, architectural, multiple valid approaches, unclear requirement. Direct: single-file fix, obvious scope, clear instruction.
feedbacks: A single-file fix with a clear cause: direct execution solves it; plan mode would only add friction.
Correct. Multiple valid approaches and an architectural decision: plan mode explores and proposes before editing.
A trivial, obvious change: direct execution.
Targeted scope and a clear instruction: direct execution.
Correct. A broad, multi-file structural change: design and approve the plan first.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: FinStack, a team of 30 .NET developers, has adopted Claude Code to generate, refactor, and test code in a microservices monorepo. The Claude Code configuration (CLAUDE.md, rules, skills, hooks, settings) is shared through git.

The repository has .claude/commands/new-feature.md (old) and, since last week, also .claude/skills/new-feature/SKILL.md (a new version of the same workflow). A developer types /new-feature. What happens?
opcoes: The command from .claude/commands/ runs, because explicit command files take precedence over skills, which are meant for auto-loading.
Claude Code asks the developer which of the two versions to use.
The skill runs: commands were merged into skills, and in a name conflict, the skill wins.
Both files run in sequence, first the command and then the skill.
questoes.explicacao: Custom commands were merged into skills: .claude/commands/x.md and .claude/skills/x/SKILL.md both create /x; in a conflict, the skill wins.
feedbacks: It inverts the rule: in a conflict, the skill wins.
There is no such disambiguation prompt; precedence is deterministic.
Correct. Both formats create /new-feature; when they collide, the skill takes precedence. It's worth removing the old file to avoid confusion.
There is no combined execution; only one definition serves the name.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: FinStack, a team of 30 .NET developers, has adopted Claude Code to generate, refactor, and test code in a microservices monorepo. The Claude Code configuration (CLAUDE.md, rules, skills, hooks, settings) is shared through git.

The /map-dependencies skill reads dozens of .csproj files and generates a report. After it runs, the main session is packed with the output of those reads and Claude starts forgetting what it was implementing. Which change to the skill's frontmatter solves this best?
opcoes: Add disable-model-invocation: true.
Restrict allowed-tools to Read and Grep.
Keep the skill as it is and run /compact right after each execution, preserving only a summary of what was read in the main session.
Add context: fork, so the skill runs in an isolated subagent.
questoes.explicacao: context: fork runs the skill in an isolated subagent (CLAUDE.md loads, the history doesn't) and returns only the result: ideal for high-volume work.
feedbacks: This only prevents the model from invoking the skill on its own; when it runs, it pollutes the context just the same.
It limits the tools, not the volume of output that enters the main session.
It patches the symptom after the damage is done and may lose details of the main task; isolation avoids the problem.
Correct. context: fork runs the skill in a subagent with its own context; the noisy work stays there and only the report comes back.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: FinStack, a team of 30 .NET developers, has adopted Claude Code to generate, refactor, and test code in a microservices monorepo. The Claude Code configuration (CLAUDE.md, rules, skills, hooks, settings) is shared through git.

The /deploy-staging skill publishes the service to the staging environment. The team noticed that Claude sometimes invokes it on its own when someone comments "I think it's ready to test". They want it to run only when a developer types the command. Which change should they make?
opcoes: Add disable-model-invocation: true to the skill's frontmatter.
Write in the description: "do not use this skill automatically".
Add user-invocable: false to the frontmatter.
Move the skill to each developer's ~/.claude/skills/.
questoes.explicacao: disable-model-invocation: true makes the skill run only through explicit invocation by the user. user-invocable: false does the opposite (only the model sees it).
feedbacks: Correct. This field prevents auto-loading by the model; the skill remains available when the user invokes it explicitly.
A probabilistic instruction in the very field that drives auto-loading; it doesn't guarantee the behavior.
It does the opposite of what is wanted: it hides the skill from the user and leaves it only to the model.
It changes the scope (personal), not the invocation mode; the model could still trigger it.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: FinStack, a team of 30 .NET developers, has adopted Claude Code to generate, refactor, and test code in a microservices monorepo. The Claude Code configuration (CLAUDE.md, rules, skills, hooks, settings) is shared through git.

The CLAUDE.md says "never edit files in Migrations/ or .env files". Even so, twice a month Claude has modified a migration already applied in production. What is the appropriate fix?
opcoes: Repeat the rule in bold at the beginning and at the end of CLAUDE.md.
A PreToolUse hook on Edit|Write that blocks (exit 2 or deny with a reason) targets in Migrations/ or .env.
Create a reviewer subagent that examines the diffs at the end of each session.
A PostToolUse hook on Edit|Write that detects changes in Migrations/ or .env and alerts the developer immediately, with the diff of the change made.
questoes.explicacao: A critical rule goes in code: PreToolUse blocks beforehand (exit 2 blocks; exit 0 lets it through). PostToolUse is for normalizing/annotating afterward.
feedbacks: The prompt is still probabilistic; the observed failure will recur less often, but it won't go away.
Correct. A safety/integrity rule needs deterministic enforcement; the hook always blocks, and the reason steers Claude toward another path.
It detects after the fact and adds complexity; the block has to happen before the edit.
PostToolUse runs after the edit has already happened: it alerts, but it doesn't prevent.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: FinStack, a team of 30 .NET developers, has adopted Claude Code to generate, refactor, and test code in a microservices monorepo. The Claude Code configuration (CLAUDE.md, rules, skills, hooks, settings) is shared through git.

The team wants every .cs file edited by Claude to go through dotnet format automatically, without depending on someone remembering to ask. Where and how should this be configured?
opcoes: An instruction in CLAUDE.md: "always run dotnet format after editing".
A PreToolUse hook on Edit|Write that runs dotnet format before the edit.
A PostToolUse hook (matcher Edit|Write) in .claude/settings.json, running dotnet format.
A PostToolUse hook with matcher Edit|Write in each developer's .claude/settings.local.json, running dotnet format on the changed file.
questoes.explicacao: PostToolUse normalizes the result after the tool runs; project settings (.claude/settings.json) are shared, settings.local.json is personal.
feedbacks: Probabilistic: Claude will forget sometimes. The request is precisely not to depend on someone remembering.
Wrong event: before the edit, the file doesn't yet have the change to format.
Correct. PostToolUse runs after every edit, deterministically; in the project settings, it applies to the whole team via git.
Right event, wrong scope: settings.local.json is personal and gitignored, so it doesn't apply to the team.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: FinStack, a team of 30 .NET developers, has adopted Claude Code to generate, refactor, and test code in a microservices monorepo. The Claude Code configuration (CLAUDE.md, rules, skills, hooks, settings) is shared through git.

Developers complain that Claude asks for permission every time it is about to run dotnet build and dotnet test. At the same time, security wants to guarantee that commands like git push --force never run. Which configuration meets both demands?
opcoes: permissions.allow for build/test and permissions.deny for git push --force, in .claude/settings.json.
Run Claude Code in bypassPermissions to eliminate the prompts, and state prominently in CLAUDE.md that force pushes are prohibited in any situation.
Use acceptEdits mode for all developers.
Ask each developer to approve the commands with "always allow" the first time.
questoes.explicacao: allow/deny permissions in the project settings: allow what is safe and repetitive, deny what is dangerous. bypassPermissions is not for routine use.
feedbacks: Correct. allow removes the friction from what is safe and repetitive; deny blocks what is dangerous; in the project settings, it applies to everyone.
It removes all controls and leaves the prohibition only in the prompt; bypassPermissions is not for routine use.
acceptEdits accepts file edits automatically, but it is not a rule for specific commands and doesn't block the force push.
It stays personal and inconsistent across developers, and it doesn't provide the block that security requires.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: FinStack, a team of 30 .NET developers, has adopted Claude Code to generate, refactor, and test code in a microservices monorepo. The Claude Code configuration (CLAUDE.md, rules, skills, hooks, settings) is shared through git.

The team is going to create a security-reviewer subagent to analyze changes for vulnerabilities, without the ability to modify anything. Which TWO statements about this design are correct? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: The subagent automatically inherits the entire history of the main session, so it's enough to ask "review what we did".
The subagent's frontmatter can set bypassPermissions so it works without interruptions, even if the main session is in default mode.
It should be defined in .claude/agents/security-reviewer.md, with frontmatter restricting the tools to read-only ones (for example, Read, Grep, and Glob).
Since the subagent's context is isolated, the delegation request must explicitly state what to review (files, goal, criteria).
To be recognized, the subagent must be listed in the project CLAUDE.md.
questoes.explicacao: Custom subagents live in .claude/agents/ with frontmatter (tools, model...). An isolated context requires an explicit prompt, and the parent's permission mode cannot be overridden.
feedbacks: False: a new subagent has its own context. 'Review what we did' fails for lack of context.
The parent's permission mode carries down to the subagent and cannot be overridden by it.
Correct. Custom subagents live in .claude/agents/ (markdown + frontmatter with tools, model, permissions...).
Correct. The subagent doesn't inherit the main conversation's history; everything it needs goes in the prompt.
Not necessary: Claude Code discovers the subagents in .claude/agents/.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: FinStack, a team of 30 .NET developers, has adopted Claude Code to generate, refactor, and test code in a microservices monorepo. The Claude Code configuration (CLAUDE.md, rules, skills, hooks, settings) is shared through git.

A developer asked Claude three times, in prose, to write a parser for the date format of bank statements ("day, month abbreviated in Portuguese, and two-digit year, sometimes with a time"). Each attempt gets a different case wrong. What is the most effective way to get unstuck?
opcoes: Rewrite the prose description with more detail about each variation of the format and explicitly ask Claude to pay attention to the cases with a time.
Switch to plan mode and ask for a plan before rewriting the parser.
Ask another subagent to rewrite the parser from scratch, without the history of the attempts.
Provide 2–3 concrete pairs of input and expected output, including the edge cases.
questoes.explicacao: Iterative refinement: 2–3 concrete input/output examples beat prose instructions, especially for formats with edge cases.
feedbacks: It stays on the path that has already failed three times; longer prose doesn't eliminate the ambiguity.
Plan mode isn't what's missing here: the scope is small and clear; what's missing is specifying the format with examples.
It changes who writes the code, but not the specification, which is the cause of the errors.
Correct. Concrete input/output examples communicate the format better than a prose description, and they cover the edge cases that cause the errors.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: FinStack, a team of 30 .NET developers, has adopted Claude Code to generate, refactor, and test code in a microservices monorepo. The Claude Code configuration (CLAUDE.md, rules, skills, hooks, settings) is shared through git.

The team is going to implement the pro rata interest calculation for a contract, with several rounding rules defined by the legal department. Previous attempts with Claude produced "almost right" code that only failed in production. Which workflow is most appropriate?
opcoes: Request the complete implementation and then ask Claude to write unit tests covering all paths of the generated code.
Write the tests with the legal department's cases first, share the failures, and iterate until they pass.
Request the implementation and manually review the code line by line before the merge.
Describe the rules in detail in the project CLAUDE.md for all sessions.
questoes.explicacao: TDD as iterative refinement: failing tests first, share the failures, iterate until they pass.
feedbacks: Tests written from the code itself tend to confirm the same errors, without the external criteria from the legal department.
Correct. TDD gives Claude a verifiable, objective success criterion; the concrete failures guide each iteration.
Manual review helps, but it is the approach that has already let subtle rounding errors through.
Task-specific rules don't belong in CLAUDE.md, and prose doesn't verify anything.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: FinStack, a team of 30 .NET developers, has adopted Claude Code to generate, refactor, and test code in a microservices monorepo. The Claude Code configuration (CLAUDE.md, rules, skills, hooks, settings) is shared through git.

A PO asked for "a reconciliation screen that works like the finance team's spreadsheet". The developer doesn't know the spreadsheet in depth, and the requirement has many gaps (tolerances, currencies, what to do with discrepancies). How should the developer start with Claude Code?
opcoes: Request the implementation immediately and fix whatever is wrong during reviews.
Ask Claude to implement the rules "most common in reconciliation systems".
Ask Claude to interview them with clarifying questions before implementing.
Paste the finance team's entire spreadsheet into the prompt, with the formulas visible, and ask Claude to replicate its behavior exactly on the screen.
questoes.explicacao: Iterative refinement: with an ambiguous requirement, ask Claude to interview you before implementing.
feedbacks: It generates code on top of unvalidated assumptions; the rework tends to cost more than asking.
It delegates a vague criterion to the model; the result will be generic and probably different from the spreadsheet.
Correct. With an ambiguous requirement, the interview technique surfaces the gaps before the code, avoiding an implementation based on assumptions.
It may help as input, but it doesn't settle the decisions that aren't in the spreadsheet (tolerance, handling of discrepancies).

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: FinStack, a team of 30 .NET developers, has adopted Claude Code to generate, refactor, and test code in a microservices monorepo. The Claude Code configuration (CLAUDE.md, rules, skills, hooks, settings) is shared through git.

A developer has three bugs to fix: a time zone error in the invoice report, a typo in a validation message, and a connection leak in the HTTP client. All three are in different parts of the code and don't interact. How should the developer ask Claude?
opcoes: One bug at a time, in sequence, reviewing each fix before moving on to the next.
All three in a single message, so Claude has the full context.
All three in plan mode, since there are several changes.
Launch three subagents in parallel, each fixing one bug without supervision.
questoes.explicacao: Related problems that interact go in one message; independent ones go in sequence, to keep the changes reviewable.
feedbacks: Correct. Independent problems go in sequence: each change stays small and reviewable.
Combining problems only makes sense when they interact; here it produces a mixed diff that is harder to review.
Each bug is targeted; the number of tasks doesn't turn simple fixes into an architectural decision.
More complex than necessary for three small fixes, and it loses the incremental review.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: FinStack, a team of 30 .NET developers, has adopted Claude Code to generate, refactor, and test code in a microservices monorepo. The Claude Code configuration (CLAUDE.md, rules, skills, hooks, settings) is shared through git.

A developer generated a reconciliation module with Claude over a long session and, at the end, asked in the same session: "review everything you wrote and point out bugs". The review came back clean, but QA found two logic errors. How can the review be improved?
opcoes: Ask in the same session for a second, "more rigorous" review.
Increase the effort of the same session before asking for the review.
Ask Claude to assign a confidence score to each generated function and focus human review on the functions that receive a low score.
Review in an independent session (or a new subagent), with the code and explicit review criteria.
questoes.explicacao: The session that wrote the code should not review it: use an independent session/subagent with explicit criteria.
feedbacks: It stays in the same biased context; insisting doesn't change the point of view.
More effort in the same context doesn't remove the bias of whoever justified each decision while writing.
Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated; the bugs were precisely where the model thought it was right.
Correct. Whoever generated the code tends not to question their own decisions (reasoning-context bias). An independent review sees what the original session rationalized.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: FinStack, a team of 30 .NET developers, has adopted Claude Code to generate, refactor, and test code in a microservices monorepo. The Claude Code configuration (CLAUDE.md, rules, skills, hooks, settings) is shared through git.

After hours in a session exploring the payment service, Claude started giving answers like "this follows typical repository patterns" instead of citing the actual classes, and it repeats questions that were already answered at the start. What should be done?
opcoes: Continue in the same session and repeat the lost information whenever Claude forgets.
Open a new session, without any context from the previous one, and redo the exploration of the payment service from scratch, now with more focus and fewer detours.
Save the findings to a notes file, run /compact proactively, and delegate high-volume exploration to subagents.
Ask Claude to read all of the service's files again to recover the context.
questoes.explicacao: Signs of degradation: vague answers, inconsistency, forgetting findings. Mitigate with scratchpad files, proactive /compact, and subagents that explore and return only the summary.
feedbacks: It aggravates the problem: more tokens in the same already-degraded context.
It avoids the degradation, but it throws away hours of findings; the right move is to persist them first.
Correct. These are signs of context degradation. Scratchpad files survive compression, a proactive /compact frees up space, and subagents keep the noise out of the main session.
Filling the context with bulk reads is the cause of the problem, not the solution.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: FinStack, a team of 30 .NET developers, has adopted Claude Code to generate, refactor, and test code in a microservices monorepo. The Claude Code configuration (CLAUDE.md, rules, skills, hooks, settings) is shared through git.

A new developer asks Claude: "figure out how the tax invoice (nota fiscal) issuance flow works". The service has more than 900 files. Which exploration strategy is most appropriate?
opcoes: Read all of the service's files first, to get the complete picture before answering.
Grep for the entry points, read them, follow imports and calls with new searches, and read only what is necessary.
Use Glob to list all of the service's .cs files and first read the 50 largest, which usually contain the core business logic.
Ask the developer to paste into the prompt the files they think are important.
questoes.explicacao: Codebase exploration: grep for the entry points, read, follow imports with grep, read. For high-volume sweeps, an Explore subagent returns only the conclusion.
feedbacks: Anti-pattern: reading everything up front uses up the context and worsens attention precisely on what matters.
Correct. Incremental exploration: grep for the entry points → read → follow the dependencies. It builds understanding without wasting context.
Size doesn't indicate relevance to the flow; it is still undirected bulk reading.
The developer is new and doesn't know which files those are; Claude has the tools to discover this on its own.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: FinStack, a team of 30 .NET developers, has adopted Claude Code to generate, refactor, and test code in a microservices monorepo. The Claude Code configuration (CLAUDE.md, rules, skills, hooks, settings) is shared through git.

After a long session analyzing the billing module, a developer wants to try two different refactoring strategies (Strategy pattern and a rules table), starting from the same analysis, without one attempt contaminating the other. What should the developer use?
opcoes: --fork-session when resuming the analysis session, creating a branch with a new ID for each strategy.
--resume on the same session for both strategies, one after the other.
Two new sessions from scratch, redoing the analysis in each one.
Ask Claude, in the same session, to "forget" the first strategy before trying the second.
questoes.explicacao: --fork-session creates a new ID from a common base, so the branches don't contaminate each other; --resume continues the same conversation.
feedbacks: Correct. --fork-session creates a new session from the common base; the branches don't contaminate each other, and the analysis doesn't need to be redone.
The second attempt would inherit the history and decisions of the first: exactly the contamination you want to avoid.
It avoids contamination, but it wastes the analysis already done (and may reach different conclusions).
The history is still in the context; asking it to forget doesn't remove anything.
